After bouncing back last week, Goldman’s Risk Appetite Indicator* fell back to −0.7 from −0.3 the prior week, and the momentum index fell to −1.2 from −0.8, both their lowest since April 2025. Still far from the -1.5 to -2.0 area under which "signals are most powerful"

*”Goldman Sachs Risk Appetite Indicator (RAI) aims to track the level of global market risk appetite and risk aversion based on various market variables. A sharp rise in the index can send a warning signal that investors have more risk appetite and are potentially exposed to a correction if consensus views are tested. Similarly, a sharp decline indicates a reduction in risk appetite, and at extreme levels it can indicate that markets may have overshot. RAI signals are most powerful when the level of risk appetite is very low below -1.5, with levels closer to -2.0 giving the clearest signal over longer time horizons, as at such levels the asymmetry of subsequent medium term equity return becomes very positively skewed. RAI momentum is designed to track short term shifts of market risk appetite, and subcomponents of the RAI.”

BofA estimates global systematic positioning fell to ~$225B, its lowest since April, from ~$290B last week and ~$365B a month ago, as the volatility spike also forced vol control funds to de-risk. 

In terms of CTAs, BofA no longer lists a sell trigger for the S&P 500 (from ~−0.1% last week), as Thursday’s post-election reversal likely took CTAs’ remaining US equity longs to flat. No triggers were listed for the Nasdaq-100 either, while the Russell 2000’s buy trigger is now +5.4% away (from +1.8%).

Positively, though, BofA is not looking for more selling from the systematic community in their base case with vol-control reloading offsetting more CTA selling:

• They see roughly no net change in a flat market (from −$15B of selling last week), as vol control adding ~$12B about offsets CTA selling of about $13B.

• +$11B of buying in an “up” market (BofA’s high-percentile path, roughly +4.1% for S&P 500 futures over five days this week; from +$37B last week), as CTA buying (~$16B) outweighs risk-parity selling (~$7B).

• −$37B of selling in a “down” market (BofA’s low-percentile path, roughly −5.2% for S&P futures this week; from −$63B last week), almost all from CTAs (~$34B), with Europe and Asia leading. That’s the smallest down-market estimate in eight weeks, though, showing the impact of the cleaner positioning.

Bloomberg has a detailed reconstruction of how Thursday’s post-midterm rout snowballed. Retail sold first, institutions piled on, then the mechanical sellers took over, and almost no one stepped in on the other side.

The end result: the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4%, its worst day since March 2020, leaving it nearly 15% below its October 6 record. The S&P 500 lost 4.4%, its worst day since April 2025. Bloomberg puts the US market value erased at $3.7 trillion.

The sequence:
▪️ Retail moved first. Net single-stock selling ranked behind only two days, both in March 2020 (Vanda Research), and JPMorgan put it at more than three standard deviations from normal.
▪️ Hedge funds and long-only managers followed, locking in gains from a strong year (Jefferies’ Mohit Kumar) and being caught offsides after taking off risk Wednesday (Goldman).
▪️ No buyers emerged. Vanda’s Viraj Patel said these are flows “we rarely see outside periods of genuine market stress.”
▪️ Then the machines. Nomura’s Charlie McElligott estimated options dealers were adding about $7 billion of selling for every 1% drop. He estimated vol-control funds needed to sell about $61 billion, with $25 billion more still left over from Wednesday (up volatility is just as bad as down volatility for that group), and leveraged ETFs another $47 billion. Trend-following CTAs sold about $13 billion of S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures, taking their exposure near the lowest in Vanda’s data.

What makes this particularly unusual is how calm things were beforehand:
▪️ The VIX started Thursday at 16.6, below its one-year average, and closed at 28.2, up 70%. Since 1990, only two VIX spikes started from a lower level and went further: February 5, 2018 (the “Volmageddon” short-volatility blowup, when the VIX jumped 116%) and December 18, 2024 (the hawkish Fed cut, up 74%).
▪️Positioning was already defensive going in. Hedge fund shorts were near a five-year high in late October, and net leverage was at a three-year low (although beta-adjusted it was more around average levels).
▪️ The damage was narrow but deep. Memory, optical networking, data-center and AI-chip baskets fell 12% to 15%, five- to six-standard-deviation moves, while the S&P 500 excluding AI names fell 2.3%.
▪️ Goldman Sachs’ memory basket is now 51% below its June 22 peak. That’s deeper than its 44% drawdown in April 2025, which took 14 months to recover. It’s also the first of nine drawdowns since 2022 that hasn’t been bought, now 136 days in.

▪️For the bears: Bloomberg counts 48 times since 1980 that the S&P 500 fell 2% or more the day after gaining 1.5%, almost all inside bear markets or crises. Only four came this close to a record high. Two recovered within 50 sessions, and the other two were in 1987.
▪️ For the bulls: Both VIX analogs ended with new S&P 500 highs, but on very different timelines. After December 2024, the next record close came about five weeks later, on January 23, 2025. After February 2018, it took about six and a half months, until August 24, 2018, with a retest along the way.

Now with CTAs and vol-control having dramatically lowered exposure, Bloomberg says the forced sellers look mostly spent. That’s the usual setup for a bounce they say.

Friday’s bounce was a start but not a convincing one. The Nasdaq rose 1.1% and the S&P 500 0.3%, both well off their highs. Decliners outnumbered advancers in the S&P 500 by about 5 to 3. A hot jobs report (165,000 versus 65,000 expected) also kept a December rate hike in play.

MarketWatch: A new report from Cambridge, MA-headquartered independent research boutique Forrester Research scrutinized the financial health of the major AI players and concluded that while a bursting of the AI bubble is not imminent, signs of strain are showing.

Their research illustrates that until September nearly all of the capital investment was paid for through operating cash but since then, the cushion is wearing thin. For example, Amazon spent $77 billion versus $42 billion of cash. Alphabet blew $9 billion more than available cash, Meta by $1.12 billion and both companies sold shares to raise capital in the last few months. Microsoft is still spending its own cash but borrowed money anyway through a filing ro raise $25 billion in bonds.

More worryingly, on the fringes of this cohort Oracle spent $1.61 per operating dollar in the year to August. The Forrester report, lead-authored by Brian Hopkins, defines a bubble as “supply built ahead of demand”. They estimate U.S. GDP needs to rise by 5% by 2035 to justify the current level of infrastructure investment.

As always, a nice update from Eric who remains bullish long term on the AI trade: 

"Remember Liberation Day? Remember the DeepSeek scare? Both caused panic. Both looked like the end of the AI trade at the time. Look where we are since then.

"The AI revolution isn’t collapsing. This is a speed bump."

He also notes that historically after large VIX spikes "Fear spikes. Then it fades. The market has a habit of rewarding those who don’t panic."

In that regard has he some stats on VIX spikes, but we also had an even more notable spike in the VVIX (the VIX of the VIX) which saw its biggest one-day percentage gain since February 2007 and its biggest point gain since Volmageddon in 2018.

We’ve had six cases since 2007 of the VIX rising at least 40% and the VVIX at least 30% on the same day. The S&P 500 was higher a month later in all six, by an average of 2.3%. At three months, though, only four of the six were higher, by an average of 2.3%. That’s no better than the S&P 500’s typical three-month gain since 2007, about 2.5%, which was higher 72% of the time, but is certainly not bear market material.

The outliers were October 10, 2018, and November 26, 2021. The October 2018 spike came as rising Treasury yields and the Fed’s hawkish push (it was a week before Powell's infamous “a long way from neutral" statement) hit tech stocks. It turned out to be the start of the fourth-quarter selloff, which took the S&P 500 down almost 20% by Christmas Eve, and the index was 6.8% lower three months later. 

The November 2021 spike was the Black Friday Omicron scare (followed days later by Powell saying it was time to retire the word “transitory” for inflation), although the S&P 500 would still peak in early January. Three months later it was down 4.8%, as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine deepened what became the 2022 bear market.

The common thread: in both misses the spike was an early warning of a macro shift, Fed tightening in particular, not a one-off scare or "speed bump" as Eric would say it is.
